name: Nabit
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Giffen, Robyn. 2015 [online 2016]. We begin to write: creating and using the first Nabit orthography. MA thesis (Interdisciplinary Studies), University of British Columbia (Okanagan). 149 pp. DOI 10.14288/1.0074444
catalog_locator: §4.3 'Phonological Analysis of Nabit', pp. 77-80: scope caveat p. 77, 'Phonologically Nabit is very similar to Gurenɛ' p. 78, tone statement p. 80; second tone statement pp. 43-44, the quoted sentence 'Based on my analysis..' on p. 44; §4.5.1.2 'Spelling Rules', p. 93; p. 10 Dakubu e-mail on final-vowel weakening (footnote 8: 'This means words have a consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel structure.')
catalog_quote: [p. 77] While a full analysis of the phonology of Nabit is not possible in the scope of this thesis, understanding the basic phonology of Nabit is important to understand the symbol selections that the NLC made. ... [p. 80] Nabit is also a tonal language with two tones, a high tone and a low tone. Tone is rarely contrastive though meaning that if a word is said with the incorrect tone it does not usually affect the meaning. Therefore, the NLC decided that marking tone on all words was not necessary, and tone markings for high tone < ́ > and low tone < ̀ > would only be written in cases where the meaning was ambiguous. ... [p. 44] Based on my analysis I discovered that although high and low tones exist in Nabit, these tones do not affect native speaker's ability to understand a word or phrase, but several speakers pointed out that when I said words with the incorrect tone they sounded wrong. ... [p. 93] The last spelling rule I addressed is the tendency to drop unstressed vowels. For example the word for fire is usually pronounced [bugəm] with an unstressed second vowel, so some people spelled it < bugm > instead of < bugum >. When I discussed it with the committee we decided that the true form of the word was [bugum] and, therefore, the second vowel should be written. This issue also arose in the practice spelling session for the word [sɛg̃ər] meaning forest.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only phonological description of Nabit says it is a two-tone (H/L) language in which tone is rarely lexically contrastive; it never states where word stress falls. The sole mention of stress is incidental: non-initial vowels can be 'unstressed' and reduced to schwa / dropped (e.g. bugum 'fire' [bugəm]), which is consistent with initial prominence but is not stated as a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Giffen (p. 9) relays M. E. Kropp Dakubu (e-mail 2012) that Talni, Nabit and Kusaal 'tend to weaken and drop the final vowel in a trisyllabic word, CVCVCV, whereas Gurenɛ usually weakens the second vowel' — a vowel-reduction difference between dialects, not a stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from elicited word lists (Swadesh 100 + extended list) and an Alphabet Design Workshop; author is an anthropologist and says 'a full analysis of the phonology of Nabit is not possible in the scope of this thesis' (p. 77).
new_statements.identity_note: Giffen 2015 describes the Nabit of the Nabdam District (Nangodi area, Upper East Region, Ghana), i.e. Glottolog nabi1240. Ethnologue/ISO 639-3 subsume Nabit ('Nabt') under Farefare [gur] = Glottolog fare1241 (Gurenɛ/Frafra); the 2014-2017 ISO request to split it (2015-014, code nbz) was rejected. Descriptions of Gurenɛ (e.g. Dakubu et al. 2007 dictionary, Schaefer 1975 phonology) therefore belong to fare1241, not to this entry, though Giffen states Nabit is 'phonologically very similar to Gurenɛ' (p. 78).
